headline: Flowers are advertising—beautiful displays designed to attract pollinators
universal_truth: Beauty often serves a purpose; what attracts attention usually offers something in return
fun_facts: Flowers evolved about 140 million years ago and quickly dominated plant life
Some flowers have patterns visible only in ultraviolet—visible to bees but not humans
Flowers and their pollinators often evolved together, each shaping the other
discussion_questions: Why are flowers beautiful to us if they evolved for insects?
What's the 'deal' between flowers and pollinators?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Flowers aren't for us—they're advertisements for bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Bright colors, sweet scents, nectar rewards: all designed to attract pollinators who carry pollen from flower to flower. Beauty here is marketing.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Plants can't move to find mates. So how do they reproduce? What problem do flowers solve, and why did they evolve such elaborate displays?

options.text: Flowers recruit mobile animals to carry pollen between plants, enabling reproduction without movement
options.response: Yes. Plants outsource their mobility problem to animals. The flower advertises; the pollinator carries genetic material. Both benefit from the arrangement.

options.text: Flowers protect developing seeds from damage
options.response: Fruit protects seeds later, but flowers solve the pollination problem first...

q1.title: Color Codes
q1.script: Flower colors aren't random. Bees see ultraviolet, so many flowers have UV patterns we can't see—landing strips for pollinators. Red flowers often attract hummingbirds, who see red well. Each color targets a different audience.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Color Codes"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Mutual Evolution
q2.script: Flowers and pollinators shaped each other over millions of years—coevolution. Long-tubed flowers evolved alongside long-tongued moths. Each changed to better match the other. They're partners across evolutionary time.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Revolutionary Success
q3.script: Flowering plants appeared 140 million years ago and rapidly dominated. Today, they're 90% of plant species. Flowers were an evolutionary breakthrough—outsourcing pollination to animals was dramatically successful.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Beauty often serves a purpose. Flowers teach that what attracts attention usually offers something in return. The most sustainable attraction is mutual benefit—both sides getting value.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 145. Tomorrow, we'll discover why plants make fruit. Until then, look at a flower and see the advertisement it really is.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Purpose of Beauty - See the Function
growTrack.activity: Look at something beautiful today—in nature or design—and ask: what purpose does this beauty serve? Who is it attracting? What's being offered? Beauty is often functional, solving problems through attraction.
